newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Nine killed in Pakistan bomb blasts.
newsitem.headline: Nine killed in Pakistan bomb blasts.

text.p: At least nine people were killed and 23 wounded by two bomb blasts on Monday in the central Pakistan province of Punjab, police said.
They said eight died and 21 were hurt when an explosion tore apart a bus near the eastern border city of Sialkot in the morning.
In the second incident, a Shi'ite Moslem activist was killed and two of his companions were injured by a bomb they were carrying exploded near the northern Punjab town of Chakwal, the police said.
The bomb explosion in the bus occurred at 6:15 a.m. (0115 GMT) in a bus travelling to Sialkot from Lakhanal near the Indian border. Many of the passengers were day labourers, hospital doctors said.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the blast and no word on its motive.
Police had picked up about 500 Sunni and Shi'ite Moslem militants in Punjab province overnight as part of efforts to quell a wave of sectarian unrest, officials in Lahore said.
More than 400 were released after questioning and 92 were detained for further investigation, they said.
The Punjab provincial government ordered the crackdown, which began at midnight (1900 GMT Sunday), following a spate of killings among rival religious groups.

In the latest attacks, gunmen killed at least five people, four of them in a mosque, in Lahore on Sunday. and a Shi'ite Moslem lawyer was shot and wounded in the arm in the southern Punjab town of Dera Ghazi Khan on Monday, local officials said.

The activists detained overnight included members of the Sunni Moslem Sipah-i-Sahaba Pakistan (SSP) organisation and two Shi'ite Moslem groups, Sipah-i-Mohammad Pakistan (SMP) and Tehrik-i-Jafria Pakistan (TJP), officials and relatives said.
The Punjab provincial government said on Sunday it would seize all literature deemed liable to fan sectarian enmity.

Sectarian violence is rife in Punjab, where militant Sunni and Shi'ite factions are engaged in a feud that officials say has killed more than 100 people so far this year, including religious scholars, lawyers and doctors.
